title: Dancing to Ellington outside Lucille Achet's shop and a lifetime contract offer
summary: Dancing outside the record shop to Ellington's Ring Them Bells brings customers in; the owner offers to manage him on a lifetime contract and take him to New York.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So I continued to do this. In the meantime I got back to the 81 Theater, to this lady's record shop, Miss Lucille Achet. That was George Roby's daughter-in-law. And he was a fight promoter, and he had Obey Bearcat Walker and a couple of more fighters. Obey was a heavyweight, and the others was -- there was a bantamweight and a welterweight, you know, and he was going to bring them up to New York somewhere, what they called up North.

Now, one of the fighters didn't want to leave the South. So he stayed back. Now, as I -- I was out in front of this lady's record shop, you know, and she had a sound system that -- and she'd play music from inside the shop, and it would come out back over the sidewalk as the people walking along, you know, attract their attentions.
So she happened to be playing one of Duke Ellington's numbers, 'Ring Them Bells', and I said, well, that's

readymade music, you know, and I was trying to learn how to dance with the music anyhow. So I tried myself out, see? And the people start to gathering round, you know, and -- 'What's he doing? What kind of feet has he got, you know? Because I didn't have any shoes on, and I had them bottle tops on the bottom of my feet, you see.

And I would kind of make the people like the music, you know, and they'd say, 'What's that he's dancing to?' You know? And I like that, you know. That's good, you know. So I say, well, 'If you go in the store there and ask that lady right yonder', I say, 'she'll tell you about it, you know.

So quite a few people stopping, you know, and going in and see about this recording, see. Then she wanted to know why this was happening, why these people were coming in asking for this music, and she saw me out there, you know. She says, 'Is that you that's causing the people coming in my store, you know? I say, 'Yes, ma'am.' I say, 'Well, they was asking me about the music that was coming out, you know, and I was out here dancing, you know.

I say, 'My mother's coming home, and I want to surprise her.' She say, 'Yeah?' She say, 'Well, keep it up. It's all right,' she says, 'but I just wanted to know.' And then she asked me about J. D., did I know a J. D. And I said, 'Oh, yes, ma'am, he's a playmate of mine, you know. She said, 'Did he teach you to dance? I say, 'Yes, yes, ma'am,

And I say, "My aunt mostly taught me how to keep time, you know, but school is out now, and so I -- I comes out. I try to make some money, you see. And she said, "Well, that's nice. Evidently the people must like what they're seeing because and they (inaudible) comes in and they ask for that particular record, she says, "How would you like to work for me?" I said, "Oh, yes, well, how could I do that?"

She say, "Well, you would have to sign a contract." I say, "A contract? What's that?" She say, "Well, I'd have to be your manager, you know, and I say, "Yeah? How long is the contract for?" She say, "Well, it would be for life." I say, "A lifetime contract, is that good?" She say, "Oh, yes, and she explained to me about the -- some of the details of the contract, and she says, you would be guaranteed work maybe six months out of the year and the other half, six months, you would get half pay.

So I ask her, I ask her where were we going to go to work, you know, and she say, well, her father-in-law was going -- getting ready to go to New York, and I would see that he take you up there. Would you like to go to New York?
